rationale: B wins because it knows where the fact line is and stops before tap-dancing over it. A's weakest move is the kept headline, "Canva bought an AI image-generation startup — now it's the engine inside an enterprise pitch," which smuggles in causality the update does not prove. B handles the same material cleanly with "Generative AI with a brand guardrail" and explicitly says the acquisition link is "plausible and unconfirmed"; that is the difference between strategist and brochure intern with a thesaurus.
gaps_in_A: "now it's the engine inside an enterprise pitch" overclaims the acquisition-to-product connection; the update only says Canva recently acquired an AI image-generation startup and is launching an AI tool.
"The acquisition and the AI-powered Enterprise launch are being connected in the same announcement" is not in the supplied facts. It may be context, but the set treats it as sourced.
It misses the finance/private-markets angle around "privately held, profitable, and last valued at $26B," which is one of the few clean non-product stories in the update.
The next step, "newsjack-detector," is defensible but not the sharpest default. For a launch angle set, the immediate blocker is customer/proof and journalist fit, not hunting for an external peg.
gaps_in_B: "Profitable and valued at $26B, Canva is now selling to the procurement office" slightly infers the buyer motion from enterprise features; it is reasonable, but it still needs procurement or sales-motion confirmation before pitching hard.

"the first product move that can be read against those two numbers" is a touch too confident. The update does not say this is Canva's first enterprise-relevant move, only that this suite is launching now.
It could have made the missing named-customer problem even more central in the kept angles, because that is the biggest press blocker across the set.
